solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Exhaust manifold initially receding in value

indicators.note: what comes initially is at the very start, so only the opening letter of the word is kept
something receding goes backwards, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: to exhaust someone is to tire them
first letter of manifold

explanation.surface: A mechanic finds a car's exhaust manifold losing value as it ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhaust manifold' reads as one car part, but 'Exhaust' is a verb (TIRE) and 'manifold' only lends its M; the pair then runs backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Merit is worth or excellence, so it is a straightforward synonym for value in the sense of deserved esteem.

clue.text: Former PM repeatedly to hinder adult play

blocks.note: John Major was British Prime Minister from 1990 to 1997
to bar is to hinder, said twice
A is the film classification for adult

explanation.surface: A former prime minister keeps getting in the way of a grown-up theatrical production.
explanation.walkthrough: MAJOR BARBARA is a George Bernard Shaw play about a Salvation Army officer; John Major supplies the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a well-known comedy by Shaw, first staged in 1905, so the clue names it by category as a play.

clue.text: Fanatical invasion involving British

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: a raid is a sudden invasion or attack
B is the standard abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A zealous invasion that the British are caught up in.
explanation.walkthrough: The one-letter abbreviation for British sits inside a word for a sudden attack.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabid describes extreme, unreasoning zeal, as in a rabid supporter, so it matches fanatical closely.

clue.text: Male with heartless jokes interrupts offensive wealthy hedonists

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter is cut out of the word
to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so these letters go inside

blocks.note: he is the male pronoun
JESTS are jokes; losing the middle S leaves four letters
the Tet Offensive was the 1968 North Vietnamese campaign in the Vietnam War

explanation.surface: A man with feeble jokes butts in on a gathering of rich pleasure-seekers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'offensive' looks like an adjective describing the hedonists, but it is a noun: the Tet Offensive of 1968 in the Vietnam War, split open to take the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The jet set are fashionable rich people who travel widely for pleasure, a set phrase for wealthy hedonists.

clue.text: Give queen chops after having taken large bite

indicators.note: once something has been taken away it is gone, so a letter is removed
to chop is to cut into, so one piece splits the other and sits inside it

blocks.note: give as a noun means flexibility or pliancy
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels
QU is a standard abbreviation for queen

explanation.surface: Chopping food for a queen once she has taken a big bite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give' is a noun here, as in the give of a mattress: PLIANCY. With its L taken away, the queen's QU cuts into what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Bite can mean a sharp, pungent flavour, and piquancy is exactly that tangy sharpness in food.

clue.text: Full agreement announced

indicators.note: what is announced is spoken out, so the word is heard rather than read

blocks.note: a pact is an agreement

explanation.surface: A declaration that everyone is in complete agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Full agreement' reads as total consensus, but 'Full' is the definition and the agreement is only its sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A packed room or bag is one that is completely filled, so the adjective means full.

clue.text: Collection of posers on TV?

blocks.note: surface reading: a group of vain people striking attitudes
setter's reading: posers are puzzling questions, and a television programme is built from a string of them

explanation.surface: A gang of show-offs parading on television.
explanation.walkthrough: A poser is both someone who poses and a difficult question; the second sense turns the TV line-up into a programme of questions.
explanation.definitionFit: A television programme in which contestants answer a series of questions is literally a collection of posers broadcast on air.

clue.text: Nervous glimpses of tracer shells, some circling

indicators.note: a glimpse is only a first brief look, so just the opening letter of each word is seen
to circle something is to go right round it, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: the first letters of these two words
some and any are interchangeable, as in 'have you any bread?'

explanation.surface: Soldiers made jittery by catching sight of tracer rounds flying round them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tracer shells' is not a hidden-word stretch; only its initial letters count, placed inside a small word for 'some'.
explanation.definitionFit: Antsy is informal, chiefly American, for restless or agitated, as if having ants in one's pants.

clue.text: Hint of childhood memory soon includes grand old man?

indicators.note: a hint is just a small first trace, so only the opening letter is kept
to include is to take in, so one word holds another inside it

blocks.note: first letter of childhood
ROM is read-only memory in a computer
anon is an old word for soon
G is short for grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: A faint recollection from childhood of a revered elderly man coming up soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grand old man' looks like a phrase for a respected elder; 'grand' gives only G, which slips inside ANON after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cro-Magnon was an early modern human of the Upper Palaeolithic, so the question mark flags a very old man indeed.

clue.text: Maybe brief jibe spin doctor spun

indicators.note: something spun is whirled round, so the letters end up in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, all fourteen letters

explanation.surface: A spin doctor's short, cutting remark gets twisted in the retelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brief' seems to describe the jibe, but with 'Maybe' it is a noun: a brief is one example of the answer, and 'spun' fits the spin doctor too well to notice.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief is a set of instructions outlining someone's duties, so it is one example of a document stating a role's tasks.

clue.text: Where one might look up who, having directed, failed to impress

blocks.clueFragment: Where one might look up who
blocks.note: in a dictionary the word 'who' is found under the letter W
to helm a film or project is to direct it

explanation.surface: Someone checks a reference book on a director whose work left audiences cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'who' is not a person here but a word to look up; in a dictionary or index you would find it under W.
explanation.definitionFit: To underwhelm is a jokey coinage meaning to leave people unmoved or disappointed, the opposite of overwhelming them.

clue.text: They rescue engineers bridging river banks in Rheims

indicators.note: a bridge spans something, so the outer word stretches over and encloses another
banks are the edges of a waterway, so only the two outside letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps
the Dee is a river in Britain
the first and last letters of Rheims

explanation.surface: Army engineers throw a bridge across a river near Rheims to save people.
explanation.walkthrough: Engineers are usually RE in crosswords, but here the fuller REME is needed to span the river. 'river banks' looks like one phrase; 'banks' belongs to Rheims.
explanation.definitionFit: A redeemer is one who saves or rescues, so the plural matches 'They rescue' as a description of people.

clue.text: Long thread contains garbage at the very end

indicators.note: the very end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept
to contain is to hold inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: yarn is spun thread
last letter of garbage

explanation.surface: A lengthy online thread with rubbish tucked away at the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective describing the thread, but it is the verb, as in to long for something.
explanation.definitionFit: To yearn is to feel intense longing for something, so it swaps for the verb long directly.

clue.text: Waylay old US president on eastern half of Pacific island

indicators.note: on a map the east is the right-hand side, so the back half of the word is kept

blocks.note: Guam is a US island territory in the western Pacific; its second half is taken
either George Bush, both former presidents

explanation.surface: An ex-president is ambushed while visiting a Pacific island.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' means placed after, so the president's name follows the half-island.
explanation.definitionFit: To waylay is to lie in wait and attack someone unexpectedly, which is exactly what an ambush does.

clue.text: Painter supporting bishop and a German composer

indicators.note: in a down clue whatever supports sits underneath, so the named piece is placed second, below the other

blocks.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
Max Ernst was a German surrealist painter
ein is German for 'a'

explanation.surface: An artist assists a bishop and a German musician.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'supporting' means placed below, so the painter comes after the bishop. 'a German composer' seems one phrase; 'a German' is EIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonard Bernstein was the American composer of West Side Story and a celebrated conductor.

clue.text: Confined by traffic bollard, one reversed to carry on

indicators.note: reversed means turned backwards, so the letters are read from the end
whatever is confined is shut inside something else

blocks.note: a unit is one
a traffic cone is a movable bollard

explanation.surface: A driver hemmed in by a bollard backs up in order to keep going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' is not I here but a four-letter word for a single thing, turned round inside the cone.
explanation.definitionFit: To continue is to keep going without stopping, the same as the phrasal verb carry on.

clue.text: Type of stance Blair first described as bad, later better

blocks.clueFragment: Type of stance Blair first described as bad
blocks.note: surface reading: Tony Blair calling some political position bad, then changing his mind
setter's reading: Eric Blair wrote as George Orwell; in Animal Farm the sheep bleat 'four legs good, two legs bad', later changed to 'two legs better'

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister first denounces a political stance, then later comes round to it.
explanation.walkthrough: Blair is not Tony but Eric Blair, George Orwell. In Animal Farm the pigs start walking upright and the slogan is rewritten to favour standing on two legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing on two legs rather than four is a way of standing, so the hyphenated adjective describes a stance.

clue.text: For viewers, it’s comical to inhale flies

indicators.note: things that fly scatter through the air, so the letters land in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An audience finds it hilarious to watch someone breathe in flies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flies' looks like insects being swallowed, but it is the verb signalling the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Iolanthe is a comic opera by Gilbert and Sullivan, a stage work that audiences watch for laughs.

clue.text: Graduates grasping right utensil that’s appropriate for high table?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a noun: the thing suited to a high table

indicators.note: to grasp is to hold tightly, so one piece clutches another inside it

blocks.note: BAs are Bachelors of Arts
R is the abbreviation for right
a tool is a utensil or implement

explanation.surface: University graduates pick up the proper cutlery for dining at high table.
explanation.walkthrough: High table is where senior members dine in an Oxbridge college hall; the question mark turns it into literally a tall table, the kind a pub or kitchen counter has.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall seat is made for sitting at a counter or tall table, so it is the item that suits a high table.

clue.text: Calm down — you have two presents

blocks.note: the present is now, and two of them are placed side by side

explanation.surface: Someone soothes an excited child who has been given two gifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'presents' suggests gifts, but it means the present moment, the time that is happening at this instant.
explanation.definitionFit: The doubled word is a soothing interjection used to tell someone to settle, just as one says calm down.

clue.text: Insufficient care of people probed by Times

indicators.note: a probe pushes into something, so the second piece goes inside the first

blocks.note: the laity are ordinary people as opposed to clergy
x is the multiplication sign, read as 'times'

explanation.surface: A newspaper investigation exposes negligence in looking after people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper investigating, but it is the multiplication sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Laxity means slackness or a lack of strictness and diligence, which is what insufficient care amounts to.

clue.text: Tranquillity surrounds current exam

indicators.note: to surround is to enclose on all sides, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: rest is peace and quiet
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A calm atmosphere hangs over the exam being sat right now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'current exam' reads as the present test, but 'current' is the electrical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: A resit is a British term for an examination taken again after failing it the first time.

clue.text: Work exploit raised huge cuts

indicators.note: in a down clue raising something lifts it upwards, so its letters read bottom to top
to cut is to slice into, so one piece enters the middle of another

blocks.note: an exploit is a deed or act
OS stands for outsize, a clothing label for huge

explanation.surface: Heroic efforts at work lead to huge cutbacks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work' is the definition: in crosswords it often means an opus, here Puccini's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosca is an opera by Puccini, and an opera is a musical work, so a specific example fits the general word.

clue.text: Pottery sensible about opening

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: sensible of something means aware of it
a gate is an opening in a wall or fence

explanation.surface: Pottery that is practical about how it is started.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sensible' here is the older sense of conscious or aware, as in 'sensible of the danger'.
explanation.definitionFit: Agateware is ceramic made from swirled coloured clays to resemble agate stone, so it is a kind of pottery.

clue.text: Almost from the start, English on high

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: ab ovo is Latin for from the beginning, literally from the egg; its last letter goes
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A remark that English sits on high almost right from the beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for the start is Latin, which a solver has to know; clipped by one letter it needs only E to finish.
explanation.definitionFit: Something above is overhead or higher up, which is what the phrase on high means.

clue.text: Upset dim goons with bitter little digs?

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over, so its letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Stupid thugs get upset by snide little remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digs' looks like jibes, but it is British slang for lodgings: rented rooms. The Goons were a 1950s British radio comedy team.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedsit is a single rented room for sleeping and living, so it is modest, small lodgings.

clue.text: Riskily name Peter, left trapped in Uruguay’s borders

indicators.note: anything trapped is held inside, so these letters go within the outer pair
the borders of a country are its edges, so only its outside letters are kept

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for name
peter is old criminal slang for a safe
L is the abbreviation for left
the first and last letters of Uruguay

explanation.surface: Dangerously naming a man called Peter who is stranded in Uruguay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter' looks like a man's name, but in old underworld slang a peter is a safe, as in a safecracker's peterman.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something unsafely means doing it in a dangerous way, so the adverbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Shrink from Leicester finally entering late

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is kept
to enter is to go into, so the letter goes inside the other word

blocks.note: last letter of Leicester
the late person is someone who has died

explanation.surface: A therapist from Leicester arrives late to a session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrink' tempts as a psychiatrist; with 'from' it is the verb, to recoil.
explanation.definitionFit: To dread something is to fear and recoil at the prospect of it, as one shrinks from a threat.
